{{Short description|Family of Runge–Kutta methods to solve differential algebraic equations}}
{{Orphan|date=August 2023}}

The '''Segregated Runge–Kutta''' (SRK) method<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Colomés|first1=Oriol|last2=Badia|first2=Santiago|title=Segregated Runge–Kutta methods for the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations|journal=International Journal for Numerical Methods in Engineering|date=3 February 2016|volume=105|issue=5|pages=372–400|doi=10.1002/nme.4987|bibcode=2016IJNME.105..372C|hdl=2117/86545|s2cid=34117796 |hdl-access=free}}</ref> is a family of IMplicit–EXplicit (IMEX) [[Runge–Kutta methods]]<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Ascher|first1=Uri M.|last2=Ruuth|first2=Steven J.|last3=Spiteri|first3=Raymond J.|title=Implicit-explicit Runge-Kutta methods for time-dependent partial differential equations|journal=Applied Numerical Mathematics|date=November 1997|volume=25|issue=2–3|pages=151–176|doi=10.1016/S0168-9274(97)00056-1}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Boscarino|first1=Sebastiano|title=On an accurate third order implicit-explicit Runge–Kutta method for stiff problems|journal=Applied Numerical Mathematics|date=July 2009|volume=59|issue=7|pages=1515–1528|doi=10.1016/j.apnum.2008.10.003}}</ref> that were developed to approximate the solution of [[differential algebraic equation]]s (DAE) of index 2.

The SRK method were motivated as a [[numerical analysis|numerical method]] for the time integration of the [[incompressible Navier–Stokes equations]] with two salient properties. First, velocity and pressure computations are segregated. Second, the  method keeps the same [[order of accuracy]] for both velocities and pressures. However, the SRK method can also be applied to any other DAE of index 2.

== The Segregated Runge–Kutta method ==
Consider an index 2 [[differential algebraic equation|DAE]] defined as follows:

:<math>\begin{align}
\dot{y}(t)&=f(y(t),z(t)),\\
0&=g(y(t)).
\end{align}</math>
:where <math>y(t)\in\R^n</math>, <math>z(t)\in\R^m</math>, <math>f:\R^{n+m}\to\R^n</math> and <math>g:\R^{n}\to\R^m.</math>

In the previous equations <math>y</math> is known as the differential variable, while <math>z</math> is known as the algebraic variable. The [[time derivative]] of the differential variable, <math>\dot{y}</math>, depends on itself, <math>y</math>, on the algebraic variable, <math>z</math>, and on the time, <math>t</math>. The second equation can be seen as a constraint on differential variable, <math>y</math>.

Let us take the time derivative of the second equation. Assuming that the function <math>g</math> is linear and does not depend on time, and that the function <math>f</math> is linear with respect to <math>z</math>, we have that

:<math>0=\dot{g}(y)=g(\dot{y})=g(f(y,z))=g(f(y)+f(z))=g(f(y))+g(f(z))).</math>

A Runge–Kutta time integration scheme is defined as a multistage integration in which each stage is computed as a combination of the unknowns evaluated in other stages. Depending on the definition of the parameters, this combination can lead to an [[Temporal discretization#Implicit-time integration|implicit]] scheme or an [[Temporal discretization#Explicit-time integration|explicit]] scheme. Implicit and explicit schemes can be combined, leading to IMEX schemes.

Suppose that the function <math>f</math> can be split into two operators <math>\mathcal{F}</math> and <math>\mathcal{G}</math> such that

:<math>\dot{y}(t)=\mathcal{F}(y(t))+\mathcal{G}(y(t),z(t)),</math>
:where <math>\mathcal{F}(y(t))</math> and <math>\mathcal{G}(y(t),z(t))</math> are the terms to be treated implicitly and explicitly, respectively.

The SRK method is based on the use of IMEX Runge–Kutta schemes and can be defined by the following scheme:

:Given a time step size <math>h > 0</math>, at a time <math>t_{n+1}=t_n+h</math>,
::for each Runge-Kutta stage <math>i</math>, with <math>0\le i\le s</math>, solve:
:::1) <math> y_{i} = y_n +h\sum_{j=1}^{i}a_{ij}\mathcal{F}(y_j)+h\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}\hat{a}_{ij}\mathcal{G}(y_j,z_j),</math> 
:::2) <math> g(f(z_i))=-g(f(y_i))</math>.
::Update the variables at  <math>t_{n+1}</math> solving:
:::3) <math> y_{n+1} = y_n +h\sum_{i=1}^{s}b_{i}\mathcal{F}(y_i)+h\sum_{i=1}^{s}\hat{b}_{i}\mathcal{G}(y_i,z_i),</math>
:::4) <math> g(f(z_{n+1}))=-g(f(y_{n+1}))</math>.
